results.content: Both aim to estimate causal effects, but they differ significantly in their level of control over the assignment mechanism and the assumptions required for valid inference. By correctly identifying and accounting for these different subject types, researchers can ensure more accurate causal inference and minimize biases in estimating treatment effects. If treatment assignment is randomized (under Experimental Design), then the observed difference in means between treatment and control groups provides an unbiased estimator of ATE:. The ITT effect is the observed difference in means between groups assigned to treatment and control:. In this case, the difference in observed means between the treatment and control groups is not [Average Treatment Effects], but Intention-to-Treat Effect. In experimental and observational studies, we often estimate the **Sample Average Treatment Effect (SATE)** using a finite sample. This decomposition clarifies the sources of error in estimating the true effect, distinguishing between sample representativeness (selection bias) and treatment assignment differences (treatment imbalance), and further separating these into observable and unobservable components.
